gloss: come near, bring near; offering; the inside, midst
summary: To come near or bring near: a person to a place, a person to another, a day to its arrival, an army to battle. Brought to Yahweh, the hiphil is the law’s verb for offering, and its noun קָרְבָּן is “what is brought near”, every gift laid on the altar (Lev 1:2; 23:8, 14); so Yahweh “brings near” the priests he chooses (Num 16:9–10) and is himself “near” to those who call on him (Psa 145:18). The noun קֶרֶב is the inside, a body’s inner parts or the midst of a people, where Yahweh walks and puts his law (Exo 34:9; Jer 31:33); Akkadian qerbu is the same word for “midst” and “innards” beside qerēbu “come near”. קְרָב “battle” is the coming to close quarters that the verb itself describes (1Ki 20:29), and the Peshitta’s Aramaic uses the root for offering, nearness and fighting alike.

words.gloss: come near, approach; bring near, present, offer
words.summary: The qal moves the subject near: to a place, to a person (also of sexual approach), to God at the altar, to battle; days and years “come near”. The hiphil brings something or someone near: an offering to Yahweh, a gift to a king, a man to the priesthood. The piel and niphal are rare.

senses.gloss: come near, approach (a place or person)
senses.definition: Move close to a place, a thing or a person; with God or his holy things, to come within the bounds he sets for approach.

evidence.note: “Do not come near (אַל־תִּקְרַב) here; take your sandals off your feet.”
Moses to Aaron: “Come near (קְרַב) to the altar and make your sin offering.”
Any of Israel’s seed who comes near the holy things while unclean will be cut off.
The censer plating is a memorial that no stranger not of Aaron’s seed should come near to burn incense.
Tribe, clan and house come near by turn to be taken by lot.
Jerusalem “did not trust in Yahweh, did not come near to her God”.
“You came near on the day I called you; you said, Do not fear.”
“Come near to my soul, redeem it.”

senses.definition: Of a man and woman, come together; the law forbids it with near kin.

evidence.note: “None of you shall come near to any flesh of his kin to uncover nakedness.”
“I went near the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son.”
Abimelech had not gone near Sarah.

senses.definition: Of an army or enemy, come up against, close with in fight; of a battle, be joined.

evidence.note: On the seventh day “the battle drew near” (וַתִּקְרַב הַמִּלְחָמָה), was joined, and Israel struck Aram.
“When you come near a city to fight against it, call to it for peace.”
“When evildoers came near me to eat my flesh, they stumbled and fell.”

senses.definition: Of days or a year, arrive soon.

evidence.note: Esau: “The days of mourning for my father draw near; then I will kill Jacob my brother.”
“The seventh year, the year of release, draws near.”
“The days draw near, and the word of every vision.”

senses.gloss: be brought near (for judgment or the lot)
senses.definition: Be brought before God to have a matter decided.

evidence.note: If the thief is not found, the owner of the house is brought near to God.
“You shall be brought near in the morning by your tribes.”

senses.definition: Cause to come close: things joined, a case presented, salvation brought near in time, a person drawn to God’s courts.

evidence.note: “I bring near my righteousness; it will not be far, and my salvation will not delay.”
“Bring them near one to another into one stick.”
“Happy the one you choose and bring near (וּתְקָרֵב), to dwell in your courts.”
“Bring near your case.”

The first of the seventh month: no work, “and you shall bring near a fire offering”.

“My קָרְבָּן, my bread … you shall keep, to bring near to me at its appointed time.”

words.summary: What is within: a body’s inward parts, a person’s inner self, and, with בְּ and מִן, the midst of a people, land or city. Its tie to “come near” is the closeness of what is inside; Akkadian and Ugaritic show the same noun for “midst” (and in Akkadian “innards”) beside their verb “come near”.

words.summary: The general word for anything brought near to Yahweh: animal, grain, gold, wood. Its Greek loan κορβᾶν is glossed by Mark himself as “a gift” (Mrk 7:11).

“When anyone brings near a קָרְבַּן of grain offering, his קָרְבָּן shall be fine flour.”

words.summary: The verbal adjective of the qal: one who comes near, mostly the stranger who comes near the dwelling and must die. Some of its tokens are also counted under the verb.

senses.definition: One coming close, to the sanctuary, to battle, or to a king’s table.

evidence.note: “The stranger who comes near shall be put to death.”
“Everyone who comes near, who comes near the dwelling of Yahweh, dies.”
“You are coming near to battle today against your enemies.”
The sons of Zadok, who come near to Yahweh to serve him.

words.summary: Twice, both times of nearness to God. Only two uses, so the word rests on the verb and adjective beside it.

senses.definition: Being near God, or coming near him, as the thing desired.

evidence.note: “But for me, the nearness of God (קִרֲבַת אֱלֹהִים) is good; I have made the Lord Yahweh my refuge.”
“They delight in drawing near to God”, while their fasting is for quarrel.

words.summary: Battle, war; in poetry and late prose. Its link to “come near” is shown in scripture itself: armies “come near” to battle and a battle “draws near” when it is joined (1Ki 20:29; Deu 20:3). Akkadian qarābu “battle” and the Peshitta’s קְרָבָא “war” and aphel “fight” are the same word.

senses.definition: Armed conflict, the engagement of forces at close quarters.

evidence.note: “Blessed be Yahweh my rock, who teaches my hands for battle (לַקְרָב), my fingers for war (לַמִּלְחָמָה).”

Hushai: “your presence going into the battle”.
“He redeemed my life in peace from the battle against me.”
“Scatter the peoples who delight in wars.”

words.summary: Biblical Aramaic, used as the Hebrew is: men come near the king or the furnace; the haphel and pael bring sacrifices near; and one like a son of man is brought near before the Ancient of Days.

senses.definition: Come close to a person or place.

evidence.note: Nebuchadnezzar came near to the door of the furnace.

“I came near to one of those standing by.”

senses.definition: Bring sacrifices to the altar.

senses.definition: Bring someone before a ruler; bring offerings to God.

evidence.note: One like a son of man came with the clouds to the Ancient of Days, “and they brought him near before him”.

That they may offer pleasing sacrifices to the God of heaven.

words.summary: Once in Biblical Aramaic. Its BDB key also counts four Hebrew tokens of קְרָב spelled alike.

senses.definition: War waged against someone.

evidence.note: The horn “made war (עָבְדָה קְרָב) with the holy ones and prevailed over them”.

words.gloss: draw near, touch; bring near, offer; fight

doctrine.statement: The law names its offerings by what is done with them: the worshipper “brings near” (הִקְרִיב) a קָרְבָּן, “a thing brought near”, to Yahweh (Lev 1:2). At every appointed time of Lev 23 Israel is told “you shall bring near a fire offering to Yahweh” (Lev 23:8, 25, 27, 36–37), the first sheaf is “the קָרְבָּן of your God” (Lev 23:14), and whoever neglects the Passover “did not bring near the קָרְבָּן of Yahweh at its appointed time” (Num 9:13). Approach itself was guarded: the unclean who came near the holy things was cut off, and the stranger who came near the dwelling died (Lev 22:3; Num 1:51; 17:28); Yahweh “brought near” only those he chose to stand before him (Exo 28:1; Num 16:9–10), and said “among those near me I will be shown holy” (Lev 10:3). Yet the psalmist calls the man happy whom God chooses and brings near to dwell in his courts (Psa 65:5), and says “the nearness of God is good for me” (Psa 73:28). Hebrews takes up the same words: the law, with sacrifices offered year by year, could never make perfect those who draw near (Heb 10:1); a better hope was brought in “through which we draw near to God” (Heb 7:19); Christ, who offered himself without blemish to God (Heb 9:14), is able to save completely those who come to God through him (Heb 7:25), so “let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith” (Heb 10:22). Peter says he suffered for sins once “that he might bring us to God” (1Pe 3:18), and the Peshitta writes it with this root: “bring us near”.

Yahweh is “near to all who call on him in truth” (Psa 145:18), and Israel was a nation with God near to it (Deu 4:7), “a people near to him” (Psa 148:14); Isaiah heard him promise “peace, peace, to the far and to the near” (Isa 57:19). Jeremiah foresaw a ruler from Israel’s own midst whom Yahweh would bring near, so that he would approach him, “for who would pledge his heart to approach me?” (Jer 30:21). Paul writes to Gentiles who were once without God and far off: “now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ”, and he came and preached peace “to you who were far off and to those near” (Eph 2:12–13, 17, quoting Isa 57:19); through him both have access in one spirit to the Father (Eph 2:18), where the Peshitta’s words for “near” and “access” are this root’s. James calls on believers, “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” (Jas 4:8).

The same root names God’s presence “in the midst” (בְּקֶרֶב) of his people: Israel asked “Is Yahweh among us or not?” (Exo 17:7), Moses pleaded “let the Lord go in our midst” (Exo 34:9), and Zephaniah promises “Yahweh your God in your midst, a mighty one who saves” (Zep 3:17). The new covenant moves it within the person: “I will put my law within them (בְּקִרְבָּם), and write it on their heart” (Jer 31:33); “a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezk 36:26). Hebrews quotes Jer 31:33 as the covenant Christ mediates (Heb 8:10).

note: Drafted 2026-11-11 from the brief, for Lev 23 (וְהִקְרַבְתֶּם 23:8, 16, 18, 25, 27, 36, 37; קָרְבַּן 23:14). ONE ENTRY: approach, offering, inside/midst and battle kept together. Evidence they belong: Akkadian has qerēbu “come near”, qerbu “midst; innards” and qarābu “battle” in one root; Ugaritic has q-r-b “approach” and qrb “midst” (Segert p. 200); scripture says armies “come near” to battle and a battle “draws near” (1Ki 20:29; Deu 20:3, 10); the Peshitta uses QRB for draw near, offer (pael), fight (aphel), war (qrābā), offering and neighbour. No merged letter in קרב, so no sound split is possible. LEFT OUT: קַרְדֹּם “axe” (BDB s.db.ac, 5 tokens) is filed in this section of BDB but its consonants are q-r-d-m, not formed from קרב; it belongs to its own entry (root key קרדמ), still to be written. Proper names (none of this root found in the brief). BDB KEYS: s.da.af and s.da.ag list the same 82 קָרְבָּן tokens, so only s.da.af is used (קֻרְבָּן Neh 10:35; 13:31 is the same word). s.da.ab (verbal adj.) overlaps the verb’s 7 “no stem” tokens. xs.ak.ab (Aramaic קְרָב) counts 4 Hebrew tokens spelled alike (Zec 14:3; Psa 78:9; Job 38:23; Ecc 9:18); only Dan 7:21 is Aramaic. The brief files Psa 65:5 also under the Aramaic verb (xs.ak.aa, “piel”); it is Hebrew and is cited only under the Hebrew piel. Verse numbers are the Hebrew text’s (Exo 22:7 = Eng 22:8; Num 16:9–10, 17:5, 17:28; Psa 65:5 = Eng 65:4; Psa 69:19; Psa 34:19 = Eng 34:18; Psa 38:12 = Eng 38:11; Ecc 4:17 = Eng 5:1). PESHITTA: words and verses from SEDRA’s BFBS word list (lexemes 2874 qurāḇā, 2875 qurbānā, 2876 qreḇ, 2877 qrāḇā, 2878 qarīḇā, 2879 qarīḇūṯā); stems from SEDRA’s English table (pael “bring near / offer”, aphel “fight”). Pointing of the Syriac lemmas in Hebrew script is mine from SEDRA’s vocalised forms (geminations not marked in SEDRA; qarrīḇā may be the better form). GREEK: κορβᾶν recorded as a loan (Abbott-Smith; Mark 7:11 glosses it “a gift”); κορβανᾶς (Mat 27:6, treasury) is noted on it, not given its own record (Abbott-Smith has no separate entry in the local data). COGNATES: Segert p. 200 checked against the scan image (archive.org leaf 227). Ge’ez qarba from Anderson–Moser only (Dillmann/Leslau not consulted). A suggested link of קֶרֶב to Arabic qalb “heart” was not followed (no evidence beyond resemblance). Arabic قُرْبَان marked possible (may be a loan from Aramaic religious use). Akkadian qarābu “battle” is Neo-Assyrian only; could be from Aramaic. Phoenician/Punic qrb not looked up in Krahmalkov.
